meta.note: A simplified family tree of major historic branches. Each branch has many sub-traditions; dates mark the conventional point of emergence, not the first appearance of every idea. 'Shared essentials' lists what the branch holds in common with the historic creeds; 'distinctives' lists characteristic teaching and practice.
sources: Philip Schaff, History of the Christian Church (CCEL)
Association of Religion Data Archives (ARDA), religion timelines

branches.name: Early Church
branches.keyEvent: Pentecost in Jerusalem (Acts 2), c. AD 30–33; the gospel spreads through the Roman world and beyond.
distinctives: Apostolic preaching summarised in a 'rule of faith' and baptismal creeds
Seven ecumenical councils, from Nicaea (325) to Nicaea II (787)
Bishops, presbyters and deacons; baptism and the Eucharist at the centre of worship
sharedEssentials: One God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit
Jesus Christ fully God and fully man
The Scriptures of the prophets and apostles

branches.name: Church of the East
branches.keyEvent: Does not receive the Council of Ephesus (431); organises under the Persian Empire and sends missions along the Silk Road to China (Xi’an Stele, 781).
distinctives: Syriac liturgy and theology (Theodore of Mopsuestia honoured)
Christ’s two natures (kyane) and two qnome in one person (parsopa)
Historic missions across Central Asia, India and China
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man

branches.name: Oriental Orthodox
branches.keyEvent: Rejects the Definition of the Council of Chalcedon (451) as too close to Nestorius; Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Malankara churches.
distinctives: Miaphysite Christology: 'one incarnate nature of God the Word', united without mixture
Ancient liturgies (St Mark, St James, St Basil) and fasting traditions
The Ethiopian church keeps the broadest biblical canon (81 books)
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man (rejecting Chalcedon’s wording, not its intent to affirm both)

branches.name: Eastern Orthodox
branches.keyEvent: The East–West Schism of 1054 between Constantinople and Rome, after centuries of estrangement (papal authority, the filioque).
distinctives: Nicene Creed without the filioque ('and the Son')
Icons venerated (Nicaea II, 787); Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom
Salvation as theosis; self-governing (autocephalous) national churches
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man

branches.name: Roman Catholic
branches.keyEvent: The Western (Latin) church after 1054, under the bishop of Rome; later shaped by the Council of Trent (1545–63) and Vatican II (1962–65).
distinctives: Primacy and infallibility of the pope; the Magisterium
Seven sacraments; the Mass as sacrifice; transubstantiation
Canon includes the deuterocanonical books; Scripture and Tradition together
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man

branches.name: Lutheran
branches.keyEvent: Martin Luther’s Ninety-five Theses (Wittenberg, 1517); the Augsburg Confession (1530).
distinctives: Justification by grace through faith alone; Law and Gospel
Real presence of Christ in the Lord’s Supper; infant baptism
Liturgical worship and hymnody; Book of Concord (1580)
sharedEssentials: The three ecumenical creeds (in the Book of Concord)
Christ fully God and fully man

branches.name: Reformed / Presbyterian
branches.keyEvent: Zwingli’s reforms in Zurich (1523) and Calvin’s Geneva (from 1536); the Heidelberg Catechism (1563) and Westminster Confession (1646).
distinctives: The sovereignty of God; covenant theology
Government by elders (presbyterian polity)
Worship ordered by Scripture; the Lord’s Supper as spiritual feeding on Christ
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man

branches.name: Anabaptist
branches.keyEvent: First believer’s baptisms in Zurich (21 January 1525) among Zwingli’s former students; the Schleitheim Confession (1527).
distinctives: Baptism of believers only; the church as a gathered, disciplined community
Nonresistance and refusal of oaths; separation of church and state
Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites and Brethren today
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man

branches.name: Anglican
branches.keyEvent: The Act of Supremacy (1534) separates the English church from Rome; Cranmer’s Book of Common Prayer (1549/1662) and the Thirty-nine Articles (1571).
distinctives: Bishops in historic succession; the Book of Common Prayer
A 'middle way' between Rome and continental Protestantism
The worldwide Anglican Communion
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man
Scripture contains all things necessary to salvation

branches.name: Baptist
branches.keyEvent: John Smyth’s English Separatist congregation in Amsterdam baptises believers (1609); Thomas Helwys returns to found the first Baptist church in England (1612).
distinctives: Believer’s baptism by immersion
Autonomy of the local congregation
Religious liberty; Second London Confession (1689)
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man

branches.name: Methodist
branches.keyEvent: John and Charles Wesley begin open-air preaching (1739) within the Church of England; the Methodist Episcopal Church is organised in America (1784).
distinctives: Arminian theology: grace offered to all
Emphasis on holiness and assurance; small-group 'class meetings'
Connexional church government; a tradition of hymn singing
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man

branches.name: Pentecostal / Charismatic
branches.keyEvent: Growing out of the Holiness movement, the Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles (1906) spreads Pentecostalism worldwide; Charismatic renewal in older churches from the 1960s.
distinctives: Baptism in the Holy Spirit, often with speaking in tongues
Spiritual gifts, healing and expressive worship
Rapid growth in the Global South
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man

branches.name: Non-Denominational
branches.keyEvent: Independent evangelical churches multiply from the 1960s (Jesus Movement, Calvary Chapel from 1965, later megachurches), drawing on Baptist, Pentecostal and wider evangelical streams.
distinctives: Local church autonomy without a denominational label
Contemporary worship; expository preaching
Usually believer’s baptism and an evangelical statement of faith
sharedEssentials: Christ fully God and fully man
